1:
The commentators agree on who the pastors are. Charles Ellicott says they are the civil rulers, not the prophets or the priests, the phrase used as the Greek poets used shepherds of the people. John Gill reaches the same result by elimination, the priests and prophets being named separately further on. Keil and Delitzsch add that this portion closes the prophecy begun in the preceding chapter, and that the noun stands without the article because the woe concerns all evil shepherds before being applied to the rulers of Judah. Adam Clarke maps the chapter first: vengeance against the pastors, then promises of deliverance, then at the ninth verse a new discourse on the wickedness of the priests and prophets, and at the close a sentence on pretenders to inspiration and on scoffers. John Calvin reports a division over the opening word, which the Septuagint and the Syriac make an exclamation, O ye pastors, and the Latin and the Targum a denunciation; the original will bear either, and he judges the second more suitable. He hears irony in the title, a pastor and a destroyer being contrary things, the honourable name conceded only to strip off the mask.

Calvin takes the prophecy as a mixture of promise and threatening. God undertakes to be propitious to the people after chastising them, so that the seed of Abraham should not be wholly cut off, and at once strips hypocrites of their confidence, since as soon as mercy is offered they apply the promise to themselves. He is careful, too, about the order of the three charges in the second verse, which he says are stated backwards: the scattering is named first though it is the last act, the driving out came before it, and the neglect of oversight, named last, caused both. Matthew Henry presses the accusation into a turn of phrase: in not visiting the flock the shepherds did in effect scatter it, and because they would not visit it in a way of duty God will visit them in a way of vengeance. Ellicott insists the charge was true literally as well as spiritually, the dispersion being the work of the rulers, who did not lead as an eastern shepherd leads but drove, and not to the fold but away into far lands.

On the gathering Calvin notices that God ascribes to himself what he had imputed to the shepherds, and separates the senses: they scattered the flock by sloth and cruelty, while he punished a people who deserved it, so that the ungodly execute his judgment without being excusable. The remnant is not all indiscriminately but a small number, and he appeals to the distinction Paul drew between the people and the remnant of grace; the dispersion he calls a purging of the church, chaff blown away and wheat laid up. Gill takes them for those who neither perished nor stayed behind, since not all returned upon the edict of Cyrus, and reports the opinion that the elect are meant. Ellicott would render their destination habitations or pastures, and says hope remained for the remnant though the sentence on the rulers was final. On the shepherds to be set up he sees a return to the theocracy, the hereditary succession broken off and power given to men who could rule, like Ezra and Nehemiah and later the Maccabees; the plural, he notes, does not limit the promise to the chief Shepherd, and the verb for setting up echoes the names of the two kings just condemned. Henry infers that if some have abused a sacred office that is no reason to abolish it, and that Zerubbabel and Nehemiah, who lived in none of the pomp of Jehoiakim and Jeconiah, were as great blessings as the others were plagues, since the peace of the church is not bound up in the pomp of her rulers.
5:
Charles Ellicott is exact about the figure. The word differs from the one used in the earlier prophecy, though the idea is the same: both mean a sprout springing from the root after the tree has been cut down, not a branch from the trunk. He would render the next clause he shall reign as king, making the Branch the subject, and notes that the prophet dwells on a sovereignty exercised personally on earth, given indeed to the Christ, though not as men expected. Adam Clarke argues that no age between the captivity and the destruction of the city saw such prosperity, and no ruler answered the character drawn here, so the passage must mean a branch out of the stem of Jesse. John Calvin explains why a Mediator is produced here at all: it was the practice of all the prophets, whenever they gave hope, to bring forward the coming of the Messiah, the promises of God being in him yea and amen. He notes that the promise is addressed to David, not to the people, as though God would keep faith with his servant rather than with an unworthy generation; and against those who make the branch a collective term he answers that the context speaks of one king.

The name given at the sixth verse divides the chapter sharpest, and Clarke assembles the evidence. The Septuagint, he reports, turned the clause so that the Lord calls him by a name, and Blayney rendered it this is the name by which Jehovah shall call him, Our Righteousness, the idiom admitting no other construction. Clarke traces the English versions: the oldest manuscript reads our righteous Lord, Coverdale has the Lord our righteous Maker, and the received wording comes from an edition printed at Rouen. He quotes Blayney’s defence, that some would be offended at losing a favourite argument for the divinity of the Savior, but that the Greek translators had rendered it so in an age when there could be no bias either way. Clarke states his own position: he believes Jesus to be Jehovah, but doubts whether this text says so, and holds that no doctrine so important should rest on so dubious an interpretation.

John Wesley takes the opposite view as flatly, calling the verse an eminent proof of the Godhead of Christ since he is here called by the divine name and justifying, which belongs to God alone, is applied to him. Ellicott stands between them, observing that the same name is given to the city in a later chapter, where it is plainly not a predicate but a watchword on her banner, and that we cannot press more here; he compares a city and an altar that bear names of God, and concludes that the identification of the King with Jehovah, and the doctrine of imputed righteousness, are applications rather than the direct meaning, which would be that the King looks to Jehovah as working righteousness. He adds that a king then on the throne bore a name of the same sense, and that his reign had been a miserable failure, so that the prophet looks to a time when the ideal would at last be realised. Calvin resists any reading that makes God the one called by the name, and rejects the parallel of altar and city as unlike the case in hand, since a Redeemer is set forth here and the name of God given to him. Keil and Delitzsch read the verse as the welfare the Branch secures by a wise and just rule, Judah blessed and Israel, meaning the ten tribes, dwelling safely. John Gill adds that the saving is from sin and from the curse of the law, and Calvin that the days of this king are not the years he lived on earth but a perpetuity, so that the salvation of the church lasts as long as the King.
7:
John Calvin reads the pair of verses as a comparison, not a cancelling. When the people were brought out of Egypt God testified his power by many miracles, and the prophets rightly encouraged the faithful by calling that deliverance to mind; here the second redemption is set so far above it that the first will not be spoken of, but the memory is not abolished, the prophet reasoning from the less to the greater, so that a favour which taken by itself deserved to be remembered for ever appears almost as nothing beside it. Out of this he draws an observation of his own that goes well past the verse: what God effects in the ordinary course of his providence is more remarkable than what he did by miracles, since the secret working of providence upon the minds of men accomplishes greater things than power put forth to reverse the course of nature, and though he performs no miracles now he works in a way more wonderful, as anyone may see who notices events with enlightened eyes. He is careful about the particles as well. The opening word is rendered therefore by the Latin, the Syriac and the received version, after this by one modern scholar and moreover by another, while a third gives surely; and the word that follows is better rendered when than that, the Greek and Latin giving and, which yields no sense.

Charles Ellicott observes that the words almost verbally reproduce an earlier passage, but with the stress moved: there it lay on the exile, here on the restoration. He reports that the Greek version omits the two verses in this place and inserts them, where they are obviously out of place, at the end of the chapter, and holds them fitly repeated here, connecting a hope before general with the personal reign of the Branch. Adam Clarke contributes only a cross reference to the earlier passage. John Gill reads the days as beginning shortly after the return from Babylon and reaching to the times of Christ, taking in the whole Gospel dispensation; on the second verse he notes that the clause may mean they shall swear by the living God, or, as the Targum has it, shall declare the power of the Lord in their redemption. John Wesley alone treats the promise as still outstanding, saying that possibly part of this prophecy remains yet to be accomplished, since they are not yet come to dwell in their own land.

Calvin takes the change of person in the second verse to be no obscuring of the sense, and finds two reasons for the clause in which God claims the driving out as his own act. The first is that the people had to be reminded of their sins, since unless they were convinced that they were chastised by the hand of God they would either have thought their exile a matter of chance or given way to murmuring, as they often did. The second is that God shews it to be in his power to restore those he has afflicted, which is the same as raising from death those he had slain; many can destroy, he says, but cannot heal the wound they have made, whereas God is at once a righteous Judge and a merciful Savior, so that as death is in his hand when he punishes, life is in his hand when he shews mercy. Keil and Delitzsch use the same place as a hinge into what follows, observing that next to the kings it was the false prophets, who flattered the carnal longings of the people, that did most to bring the realm down, so that the prophet passes directly from the wicked kings to rebuking them; judging from the substance, they add, the second discourse belongs to the same time as the first.
9:
Almost every voice makes the first two words a title, not part of the sentence. John Gill reports that the Latin renders them concerning the prophets and makes a stop there, agreeing with the original. Adam Clarke says the same, notes that two modern editors print them so, and dates the discourse probably to the reign of Jehoiakim. Charles Ellicott finds the abrupt transition proof of a new section, the Hebrew order and punctuation showing it more clearly, and calls the whole passage the complement of the one denouncing the civil rulers. John Calvin is the exception. He surveys the versions: the Greek attaches the words to the preceding verse where they yield no meaning, the Latin makes them a heading, the Syriac joins them to what follows; he takes the last course himself. On the description that follows he is minute. Bones are tied by sinews so that they may not be moved, and the loosening of one renders the whole body almost useless, so that the prophet expresses the most painful perturbation of mind, what was firmest in him made feeble. The comparison with a drunken man he takes further: drunkenness is like a grave that holds the whole man.

Matthew Henry divides the trouble in two. The prophet grieved first over the prophets and their sin, the false doctrine they preached and the lives they lived, and above all over their use of the name of God, the dishonour done to that name being the greatest grief imaginable to a gracious soul; and second over the judgments coming in like a deluge, for even those who have God for them cannot but tremble at the misery of those who have God against them. John Wesley reads the stupefaction as coming from two directions, the wrath ready to be revealed and the words the holy God had put into his mouth; Clarke puts it more briefly, that the prophet was terrified by his own message. Ellicott counts four clauses of horror before the cause is given, the contrast between the words of Jehovah and his holiness and the wickedness of priests and prophets. Calvin, observing that Jeremiah was wise and courageous, takes the violence of the description as a measure of how monstrous the thing was.

The tenth verse gives the reason, which Calvin turns into a rule for teachers. Where men follow what God commands, vehemence is foolish, and those who work up a fervid zeal when there is no need are nothing but apes; but where things are in confusion vehemence is wanted, and these prophets could not have kept silent unless they were logs of wood. The more liberty men take in sinning, he concludes, the more sharply faithful teachers ought to reprove. On the adulterers the voices divide. Ellicott holds that the context requires the word to be taken literally and not of the spiritual adultery of false worship, the prophets and their followers being personally profligate. Clarke takes the other view, that idolaters are meant, breaking faith with God as an impure wife does with her husband. Gill allows both, and Wesley says all species of uncleanness are comprehended. On the next word Calvin reports that it properly means swearing, though some render it execration, the old versions dividing between on account of these, of a curse, and of false swearing; Ellicott prefers because of the curse, what comes from Jehovah for the wickedness of the people, and refers the mourning of the land to a drought, as Clarke does to dearth. Keil and Delitzsch read the clauses as the land withering under a curse. On the last clause Ellicott is sharpest: the word means might or valour, and what they exulted in was might and not right, which Wesley applies to their rule and government and Henry to a heart set to do evil and not valiant for the truth.
11:
John Calvin makes the eleventh verse the explanation of the silence complained of before. It ought not to seem strange that the prophets said nothing when they should have cried out, since they were guilty themselves, and freedom of speech comes only from a good conscience. Hypocrites who indulge themselves are often severe against others, but no one can honestly cry out against wickedness except the man who is innocent, since whoever condemns others seems to make a law for himself. He notes that a man may live honestly and still connive at the wickedness of others, and that the charge here is double, that these men were mute and did not undertake the cause of God; then he traces the cause, that they dared not speak against crimes with which they were more loaded than the common people. On the verb he prefers a transitive sense against the old versions: the Greek and the Latin render it passively, that prophet and priest have become defiled, but the word is most commonly transitive and the context favours it, so that they have defiled the land, the house of God being then set against the land as a second scene of the same wickedness. What was found in the Temple, he says, was priests practising a kind of merchandise under cover of the priesthood and prophets adulterating the worship of God, religion being to them a means of gain.

Charles Ellicott reads the pairing of prophet and priest, as elsewhere in the book, as two orders playing into each other’s hands, and thinks it probable that the sins of Ahaz and Manasseh had been repeated under Jehoiakim, the worship of other gods carried on beside that of Jehovah, with shameless greed or a more shameless profligacy, like that of the sons of Eli, as its natural accompaniment. Adam Clarke puts the whole charge in a sentence, that they had introduced idolatry into the Temple itself, and John Gill refers the profaneness to the sins already named.

The twelfth verse turns to the sentence, and Calvin takes it as figurative from the first word. By their way he understands the means they thought best, as elsewhere what is deemed delectable is called the table of the wicked; so that when they thought everything prosperous, as though crossing a plain, they would find themselves on slippery ground. He notes an ellipsis, the word way being left out before the noun for slippery places, which is a plural reduplicate expressing the extreme, a way wholly slippery. He is firm that the word is not darkness but thick darkness, and that it belongs to the slippery way, as the Targum and all the versions but the Syriac take it; Blayney followed the Syriac and rendered that they should be thrust into darkness and fall therein, which Calvin says spoils the force of the passage. What he wants is a doubling of the evil: a man may stand on slippery ground and take care of himself when he sees the danger, but when darkness is added, one who can neither stand nor move can hardly do other than fall. Gill draws the same picture without the philology, a man walking on a dark night without lantern on a slippery road, scarcely able to keep his legs and unable to see where to step, and adds that such are blind leaders of the blind. On the closing phrase Ellicott observes that the prophet returns to his characteristic word for the time appointed by the divine Judge, and that the language of the verse flows in upon him from older scriptures. Calvin ends on the same phrase with a warning about delay: the year of visitation is the time God has determined within himself, and though he defers punishment, when his despisers have long abused his forbearance he begins suddenly to thunder.
13:
The passage works by comparison, which John Calvin makes its whole point. The prophets who had corrupted worship in the north are set beside those at Jerusalem who wished to appear more holy, the effect being to show that men who sought to be deemed the faithful ministers of God were by far the worst. Those are mistaken who take the first word as depravity, since they miss that the wickedness of those who thought themselves best is enhanced by the contrast: the prophets of Samaria had long been condemned, and none at Jerusalem dared defend them, while the southern kingdom wished to be thought pure. Its prophets were not merely foolish; they designedly subverted all religion. On the word itself Calvin sets out the versions, which give iniquities, fatuity, falsehood and impiety, and one modern rendering, that which was disgusting; he judges it to mean what is crude and untempered, and so absurd, fatuity being its best sense here, since to prophesy by Baal was an effect of infatuation. Charles Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch agree, the one glossing it unsavoury and so foolish, the others unsalted and so irrational; John Gill makes the point by an image, salt that has lost its savour. Adam Clarke adds only that the folly was no wonder, their religion being a system of corruption, and John Wesley that they pretended to have their instructions from Baal.

Ellicott states what made the southern prophets worse: a claim to prophesy in the name of Jehovah joined to flagrant breaches of his law was more hateful than the open recognition of Baal. Keil and Delitzsch say they strengthened the wicked not by their pretences only but by their lives, so that no one turned from his wickedness. Gill notes that the word for the horrible thing means what makes the hair stand on end, or else what is filthy. Calvin takes an unusual line on the adulterers, holding against expositors who find a change of number that the clause describes the people, not the prophets, who are condemned for dissimulating when they saw adulteries and frauds prevailing, and for patronising the wicked. Shame weakens the hands as fear does, he adds, so that in removing both these men strengthened the wicked, giving them confidence to rush more freely into evil. He confines the comparison with the cities of the plain to the citizens of Jerusalem, and takes it of their punishment as well as their crimes, there being no more hope of pardon for them than for the Sodomites. Clarke says the same more briefly, calling them incorrigible sinners who will as surely be destroyed.

On the sentence of wormwood and gall Calvin hears his earlier figure, that the table of these men becomes a snare: the ungodly think they can escape by their arts, but though a table be prepared they will find on it only poison and gall, since as evils are turned to the benefit of the children of God, so everything must turn out to the ruin of his despisers. The last word of the verse divides him from Ellicott, who holds that the root meaning is veiling, and so simulated holiness, but that the associations of the word attached to it the further sense of a hypocrisy that desecrates, so that profaneness is the best rendering. Calvin answers that the word is properly pollution, as the old versions give it, that the Targum wrongly makes it flattery, and that the received profaneness and a modern perverseness are alike incorrect, the pollution meant being the idolatry already named. He knows that making the whole land polluted from Jerusalem outward would be thought too severe, and defends it on the ground that the lamp of God still remained there and the light of sound doctrine was not put out: they professed to obey the law, and were much worse than others.
16:
John Calvin feels the weight of the command. To forbid the people to hear the prophets must have seemed severe, for he concedes the sacred name and then discredits those who bear it; and he is not speaking of magicians alien to the people of God, nor of foreigners, nor of the prophets of Samaria, but of men who appeared daily in the Temple and boasted that they were divinely chosen and brought only what God had committed to them. The simple, he says, must have asked why God suffered such men to hold a place in the Temple at all. His answer is that everyone who truly fears God will exercise his mind to distinguish the false prophet from the true, and that God never leaves his people destitute of discernment when teachers contend on both sides, provided they submit humbly to his word. On the wording he takes the clause literally as infatuating you are they, noting that the Greek makes the prophets frame a vain vision for themselves while the Latin and Syriac keep nearer with they deceive you.

Charles Ellicott puts the same clause as a test. To make vain is to befool, and the next verse shows how, since they filled the people with hopes of peace; this was then, as always, the crucial test between true prophet and false, for the one roused the conscience and caused pain by his reproofs while the other soothed men with a false assurance. They invented a vision, he says, that never came from the mouth of Jehovah. Adam Clarke defines them the same way, as those who promise safety without requiring men to forsake their sins, and John Wesley draws the general rule, that people are under no religious obligation to hear anything but the revealed will of God. John Gill says only that the hearers should stop their ears and give no credit.

At the seventeenth verse Calvin finds another mark of the false prophet, that he flatters the ungodly, and works the grammar closely. The word for saying is doubled, which he takes as emphatic of boldness, so that they boldly say; and against two scholars who attach the participle to the preceding verse he answers that the idiom will not bear it, a participle often preceding a verb in the future but never following it, and that no version supports them. He notes a second division, over whether the clause naming the despisers belongs to what precedes, as the Greek and Arabic take it, or stands separate, as the Latin, Syriac and Targum have it; the Hebrew admits either, but since the Lord seems to be the speaker he prefers the second. He adds that the word vision is conceded to these men improperly: the prophet might have said simply that they brought forward the falsehoods they had devised, but he uses a term of high import, meaning they were only apes while they prattled of visions. Ellicott has a philological point that cuts deeper. The verb used here for the divine speech is not the formula the true prophets use, and he takes this to indicate that the men he condemns put the message of God on a level with a man’s everyday utterance, so that they stood self-convicted by the phrase they used; the word rendered imagination he glosses stubbornness, and observes that the tendency of their preaching was to confirm the people in their sins rather than lead them to repentance. Gill notes that they kept company with scoffers because their doctrine met approval there, the Greek version reading it of those who put away the word of the Lord. Keil and Delitzsch draw the inference the chapter moves towards, that men who prophesy peace to the despisers of God are not sent by him, since had they stood in his counsel and learnt his word they must have published it.
18:
The question at the eighteenth verse is read two ways, and John Calvin says the usual way is wrong. It is commonly taken as condemning the false teachers for not attending to the word of God, but he holds that interpreters have been much mistaken: the passage shows how insolently they opposed the true servants of God. He puts the taunt into their mouths: these men announce pestilence and war and famine as though they were angels sent from heaven, but have they stood in the counsel of God? He admits what militates against his reading, that the false prophets themselves claimed a divine revelation. John Wesley agrees that they seem to be the words of the false prophets, asking which of those who prophesy such terrible things is a privy counsellor to God. John Gill reports both readings and prefers the second, that they are insulting the true prophets for taking too much upon them. Adam Clarke reads it flatly as God speaking, asking which of them ever received a word of prophecy from him. Charles Ellicott attends to the noun: better the council, the assembly of chosen friends with whom a man shares his secret plans, and asks whether any of these men had been called into it. Calvin adds that the image is of a man admitted to his sovereign’s council chamber and then commissioned to transact the business.

On the storm the voices converge on the weather. Calvin holds that storm is the more suitable rendering, and that the word after the divine name belongs to it, giving a hot tempest, the burning winds of the south in view; Clarke names the wind as the hot pestilential blast from the south. Calvin presses the second word further than anyone: the tempest is not merely grievous but pregnant, in travail, and being as it were in labour it bursts upon the head of the wicked. Ellicott reaches the same effect by another road, rendering it a whirling storm that shall whirl down upon the heads of the wicked, the first noun being generic and taking its force from the word the received version renders grievous, which rightly means whirling. Gill keeps to the plain sense, that the whirlwind is his fury, coming suddenly and appearing in the invading army, and draws the conclusion the passage wants: the false prophets were plainly not in the counsel of God, since they promised peace while a storm gathered.

The twentieth verse answers two hopes at once. Calvin says the hypocrites comforted themselves that the punishment would be light and soon over, and that God was dallying whenever he denounced ruin, since they did not believe his word would be fulfilled; against both he sets the declaration that the anger will not turn back until it has done its work. God does not speak as men do, whose tongue outruns their purpose; his prophetic word is sure evidence of his hidden purpose. On the thoughts of his heart Calvin is careful: we must not imagine God reflecting on this and that as things come into his mind, for such a gross idea cannot suit his nature; the heart is a metaphor for that fixed and unchangeable counsel he declared by his prophets, and it is no small commendation of prophetic doctrine that God has as it were joined his heart to his mouth. Ellicott glosses the latter days as the end of the days, the then distant future of the exile and the return, when men would look back and see the anger had done its work of chastisement and discipline. Wesley and Gill both hear a messenger in the clause, sent on an errand and not returning until it is done, and Wesley adds that they shall consider it perfectly when it is too late; Clarke gives it as a warning that a short time will determine the matter.
21:
John Calvin states the objection that gave the passage its force. Jeremiah stood alone while the false prophets were many, and common sense says a hundred persons should be believed rather than one. His answer is that the question is not of men or their authority but of who sends them, so that if God is the author of his mission then he, though alone, is superior to the whole world. Two things, he says, prove a true minister: a divine call and faithfulness in discharging it. Charles Ellicott catches the image in the verb: messengers who rush out as though from the council chamber of the king, on a mission of their own appointing, without waiting for the Master in whose name they profess to come. John Gill requires both an external call from the church and an internal call from the Lord himself, and Adam Clarke says they ran not to save souls but to profit themselves, warning that churches with legal emoluments are always in danger of being overrun by self-interested priests.

The twenty-second verse supplies a test, which Ellicott examines. The mark of a true mission is seen in results: are the people better or worse for the prophet? Then he raises the difficulty himself, whether this is always a test, and whether the work of Jeremiah was successful in that sense. His answer is that true teaching seldom fails altogether, and that where it seems to fail it rouses men from lethargy even if only to antagonism, being never satisfied with speaking smooth things. Keil and Delitzsch put the conditional plainly: had these men stood in the counsel of God and made the people hear his words they must have turned them from their evil way. Calvin adds that God had delivered the sum of all truth in the Law, from which the prophets drew whatever we read in their writings, so that none may plead ignorance, the cause of error being not sloth only but perverseness in neglecting what is set plainly before them. He notes that the Greek has no clause answering to the opening if, and that the Latin and Targum turn the second clause oddly into the first person.

On the questions about nearness Calvin finds the self-delusion of hypocrites exposed. They are torpid in their vices because they suppose they can blind the eyes of God, imagining him like a man of defective sight who sees what is near but not what is far off. He accuses the Greek translators of reversing the sense outright, making God near and not afar off, a sentiment true in itself but not what is meant here. He renders the next verse potentially, can a man secrete himself in secrecies, and reads the plural heavens, the visible and the invisible; and he insists that the seeing of God has reference to his judgment, its purpose being that he may call to account whatever men do. Ellicott says the false prophets acted as though God were far away and out of sight, not caring what men did, as if their affairs came under a colonial department, whereas the true prophet feels him equally near and equally God in all places; the word omnipresence has grown so familiar as almost to lose its power, though the fact when realised is as awful now as ever. Clarke reduces it to a sentence: they acted as if he could not see them. Matthew Henry gathers up the section: men cannot hide from the all-seeing eye, and should not call their foolish dreams divine oracles, their promises of peace being no more comparable with the promises of God than chaff with wheat; the unhumbled heart is like a rock, and if not melted by the word as a fire will be broken by it as a hammer. Gill adds that darkness and light are both alike to God.
25:
John Calvin puts the difficulty as the hearers would have felt it. The prophets disagree, both sides claim an illustrious title and affirm that they were sent by God; what then are we to do? His answer is that God meets the objection by declaring that he knows what the false prophets boast, and that it has been his will in every age to try the faith of his servants by allowing his name to be falsely pretended. John Gill notes that men who supposed God distant could deceive the people but not him. Charles Ellicott sets the dream in its history: dreams had their place among the recognised channels of revelation, but their misuse brought them into discredit, so that the law tested the dreamer of dreams no less than the prophet by whether his teaching agreed with it; and the doubling of the words represents the affected solemnity with which these men proclaimed their visions.

The twenty-sixth verse is hard to construe, and two answers are offered. Ellicott reports that the Hebrew gives a double interrogative, how long, and then whether it is in the heart of these prophets, and mentions a conjectural alteration reading how long is the fire in the heart of the prophets. Gill reaches the double question without the conjecture, taking the opening as a short abrupt exclamation with a stop after it, and the rest as asking whether there is anything at all in the heart of such men; he answers that there is nothing good. Calvin is sharper against the emenders. Correctors have been busy with the first words, he says, without the authority of any manuscript or early version, and where a meaning is present, and a striking one, conjectural emendations are to be repudiated; three scholars have their corrections and we can do without them. To be in the heart, he explains, means to be resolved, though it can also mean to delight in a thing; so the exclamation wonders at their perseverance and the question asks whether they are settled in it. The point, for him, is that they did not err through ignorance but rose up as if by design to suppress the truth.

At the twenty-seventh verse Calvin canvasses the versions of the verb, which give think, wish, study and counsel, and prefers design; the name to be forgotten is the revealed name, God as he has made himself known in his word. From this he draws the inference that gives the chapter its edge. These men were not open enemies of the Law: they held that the only true God is to be worshipped and that there was one legitimate altar, and on those points there was no controversy; their crime was the double one of running unsent and bringing their own inventions. Hence two evils are to be avoided, the open one in which truth is turned into falsehood, and the more hidden and more dangerous one in which some appearance of true religion is kept while men are drawn away from the fear of God. Ellicott makes the comparison do the same work, holding that open idolatry and false claims to prophecy stand on one footing, the misuse of the name of Jehovah being as bad as the older worship of Baal. Adam Clarke uses the occasion to say how a true dream might be known. Dreams were anciently reputed a species of inspiration, and though many mistook the workings of their own imagination in sleep for revelation, God has often revealed himself that way, and such dreams were easily distinguished: they had no connection with gratifying the flesh, they contained warnings against sin and excitements to holiness, they were consecutive and well connected, and they possessed the intellect rather than the imagination. Gill adds that the Greek and Arabic read the clause of the law of God rather than his name.
28:
John Calvin reads the twenty-eighth verse as an answer to a temptation, not a rule about dreams. The faith of many might have failed at seeing a conflict in the very Temple of God, and many threw aside all concern for religion, concluding that it was better to care for nothing. To that the verse is the remedy: the fallacies of false prophets must not impede the servants of God or prejudice his word, and those do him wrong who plead the controversies that tear religion as a licence for their impiety. John Gill makes the address precise: the words are directed not to a true prophet but to a false one: if he has dreamed, let him tell it as a dream, the fruit of his own fancy, and not impose it on the people as a revelation. Charles Ellicott finds the point in the contrast between the real and the counterfeit: let the dreamer tell his dream as such and the prophet speak the word truly, and it will be seen that one is chaff and the other wheat, one worthless and the other sustaining life. Adam Clarke cautions against mixture: equivocal matters are not to be mingled with positive revelation, nor a dream taken for the inspiration prophets receive when reason, judgment and spiritual feeling are in full exercise, and John Wesley compresses it: there is as much difference between the will of God and their dreams as between chaff and wheat.

On the twenty-ninth verse Clarke and Calvin arrive at the same emendation independently. Clarke suspects, with Blayney, that the word rendered thus once meant strength, as the Targum understood it, so that the question runs whether the power of the word is not like fire, as the writer of the Epistle to the Hebrews may have read it. Calvin says the particle seems meaningless as it stands, that the Latin omits it and the Greek and Syriac render it behold, and that one scholar took it for a noun meaning burning or a misprint of the word for power, which two others adopt and the Targum supports.

On the figures the readings diverge. Calvin distinguishes strictly by the hearers. The natural use of the word is to bring salvation, and hence it is called food, but to the reprobate it turns to poison: those who receive it with docility find nourishment, the ungodly a fire that consumes and a hammer that breaks them. Even for the faithful, he adds, it is fire and hammer, but a refining rather than a devouring fire, and a hammer that subdues the depraved affections without breaking those who submit; the rock is broken because the reprobate will not hear correction. Ellicott takes the fire first of the prophet himself, out of his own experience, since the true word burns in the heart and will not be restrained, and when uttered consumes evil and purifies good; and as the hammer breaks the rock, so it shatters the pride of man, and the heart that hears it rightly is broken and contrite. Gill divides the figure by the two parts of the word, the law being a fiery law, quick and piercing, penetrating the consciences of men, and the gospel being fire for the light by which sinners see their impurity and the way of salvation, and for the heat that makes the hearts of saints burn. Clarke ends with two warnings of his own. The first is that none should think the scriptures sufficient of themselves to convert without the Spirit, since fire must be applied by an agent and a hammer wielded by a workman; the second is drawn from the mines, where ore is roasted before crushing, as he had seen tin stones roasted in Cornwall before going under the hammers of the stamp mill, the fire driving off the arsenic so that the rock could be powdered.
30:
Adam Clarke counts three cases that drew disapproval: prophets who stole the word from a neighbour, getting intelligence from true prophets and publishing it as their own; prophets who used their tongues, giving their own counsels as revelations under the formula of an oracle; and prophets who made up false stories and called them dreams. Charles Ellicott reads the first as a want of personal originality: the oracles of the dreamers were patchworks of plagiarism, borrowed from men of their own time as false and unreal as themselves, so that the clique of false prophets repeated each other’s phrases with a wearisome iteration. John Calvin thinks that forced. The words stolen were God’s own, and the prophet would not have called the faithful servants of God a neighbour; what is pointed at is a set of secret arts, men agreeing together what to say and then each declaring it to the people as though he had it from heaven. His own view is that these were words committed to the people and stolen by being made void, as seed sown by the wayside is stolen. John Wesley agrees that they conspired what to say and so stole one from another.

The second case turns on a verb. Ellicott renders it literally, that they take their tongues, and finds no adequate evidence for the marginal rendering that they smooth them; the scornful phrase marks the absence of true inspiration, since these men plan their schemes and take the tongue as the instrument for carrying them out. He adds that the formula they used was not the ordinary word for speaking but the one that marked a speaker delivering an oracle, used elsewhere only of God, which the prophet turns on them in stern irony. Calvin gets there by a longer road. Almost all interpreters, he says, take the verb to mean rendering sweet or soft, and so condemn these men for flattering the wicked for gain; but since the verb properly means to take, and sometimes to raise on high, he sees no reason to make it a metaphor. They raised the tongue: they elevated themselves and boasted in high terms that the office of teaching had been committed to them. He rejects a proposed transposition of two letters that would give the sense of smoothing, and reports the Greek, which has them send forth prophecies of the tongue, the Syriac, that they pervert their tongues, and the Targum, that they prophesy according to their own heart. All the prophets used the added formula, he says, to show they spoke only what they had received from above, so that the elation of these men lay wholly in claiming that God himself had spoken. John Gill notes only that these are the same men under another character.

On the third case the difficulty is a single noun. Ellicott takes the false dreams to be either dreams with nothing answering to them in fact or merely the form in which the deceiver works out his plans, and glosses the word rendered lightness from its use of what is unstable as water, its force being the gushing out of water; here it points to the babbling of these men, and he recalls the English poet who described a hollow and pretentious eloquence poured out in one weak, washy, everlasting flood. Calvin works over the same word, reporting that the versions give errors, miracles, lasciviousness and rashness, and that although he once took it for licentiousness he now makes it an overflowing in words, a vaunting. From the denial that follows he draws the rule the chapter has been building to: whatever is without the command of God is like the wind and will vanish, so that falsehood and levity stand on one side and his command upon the other, and no one is of any account except he faithfully declares what he has received.
33:
The last section turns on a single word, whose history Charles Ellicott gives. The English keeps the literal meaning, something lifted up or borne, but the word passed through many shades and became a received term for a solemn utterance, and Isaiah brought it into currency, employing it a dozen times as the title of a prophecy. Jeremiah never uses it of his own messages, probably because it had become a favourite formula with the false prophets. Here he parts from everyone else in the chapter, thinking this more rational than the assumption that the false prophets flung the word at Jeremiah in mockery; and at the next verse he says the language put into their mouths is not derision but boastful assumption, for which the boaster will be punished. Matthew Henry takes the opposite view, at length. The sin charged is bantering the prophets and their dialect. It was a word they used seriously, to show what a weight the word of God was upon their spirits; the scoffers made a jest and byword of it, so that the prophets could no longer make anyone serious with it. It has been the artifice of Satan in all ages, he adds, to obstruct sacred things by turning them into sport, so that mocking the messengers baffled the messages.

He answers a charge the scoffers may have brought, that the word was newly coined and not in the lexicons in that sense: if men form new phrases in other parts of learning, why not in divinity, and especially since the Spirit of God is not tied to our rules of speaking. He turns their complaint round: they make the word a burden to themselves and then quarrel with the ministers for making it a burden to them, as the scoffers of later days slight heaven and reproach faithful ministers for preaching hell. John Calvin agrees that the phrase was a jeer repeated as a proverb in the streets, coming not from the common people only but from prophets and priests; the devil, he says, gains his whole object when he can make the word of God hateful or contemptible. Adam Clarke and John Wesley read it the same way, Clarke calling the questioners plain mockers and Wesley saying the corrupt priests would ordinarily mock the true prophets. John Gill lets the question come from any of the three orders.

Ellicott hears the answer as scorn returned: they had asked with affected grandeur what burden the prophet had, and he repeats the question with a deeper scorn; a different division of the words, which the Greek and Latin adopt, yields instead that they themselves are the burden. He would render the next clause I will cast you off, playing on the root: they have made themselves too grievous to be borne, and Jehovah will disburden himself of them. Keil and Delitzsch put the condition plainly: if they persist, the threatened punishment will certainly come. On the substitutes Ellicott says the prophet calls men back to simpler terms less open to abuse, an answer when men came with a question and a word of the Lord when none was asked. Calvin explains why the word was forbidden: it had become an obstacle that closed the way, so that they got no benefit from what they heard, and God bids them come with sincere hearts instead. He ends on a distinction: what is bitter in prophecy is accidental, for God has nothing in view but to call men to salvation; as a sick man turns wholesome food into poison, the cause being in himself, so it is our own fault when the word becomes a burden. Clarke says the same in a line, that they called all the messages of God burdens and so they would be, whereas used rightly they would have been blessings.
37:
Charles Ellicott notes that the thirty-seventh verse repeats an earlier one with one difference, that the simpler form is to be used when men come to the prophet as well as when they speak to one another, the affectation of big words being out of place in either case; and he draws the whole passage together as a protest against the hypocrisy that shows itself in cant, in solemn words which have become hollow and unmeaning. John Calvin turns the same verse into a rule for hearers. If we wish to profit in the school of God we must beware that our minds are not preoccupied by any corrupt feeling, for the reason his word stirs a bitter spirit in us is that some lust or passion has corrupted the judgment. There is but one cause why the word injures instead of profiting, that we are not teachable, sloth or contempt or ingratitude bearing rule in us; the verse also clears his faithful servants, since there is nothing wrong in the prophets when their doctrine fails to please. John Wesley asks only that they speak to the prophet reverently, and John Gill takes the address to cover everyone who came to enquire.

Calvin anticipates an objection, that God seems too indignant, having taken such offence at one short expression; the word had been borrowed from the prophets, and a single word might look an insufficient ground for so heavy a sentence. His answer is that they had often been warned not to use it, so that they had not erred inconsiderately as men do who speak rashly, but the perverted phrase proceeded from a settled wickedness and a wish to fix a mark of disgrace on the word of God. Ellicott adds only that the opening is better rendered if ye say.

The sentence plays on the disputed word, and Gill notes an elegant play between the verb rendered forget and the noun rendered burden which another language will not easily express. Adam Clarke follows Blayney in rendering that God will take them up altogether and cast them off together with the city, and puts the figure plainly: they are a burden to him, and he will take them up and cast them off, as a man weary of his load throws it from his shoulders and bears it no more. Calvin reaches the same figure by another route. Most interpreters, he says, derive the verb from one root, but he doubts that, since the noun for burden comes from the root meaning to take away; as the proverb ran that prophetic doctrine always brought some burden, God answers that he will take them away, so that they who burdened his word with indignity are treated with indignity themselves. If anyone prefers the sense of forgetting he may follow his own judgment, but Calvin finds that explanation unmeaning. He goes further, observing that the variety of the versions seems to intimate some derangement of the text, which as it stands is not according to the Hebrew idiom; supposing a single word misplaced makes the sentence grammatical, and he offers a rendering on that supposition, that God will carry them off and let them go, dismissing them and the city from his presence. On the everlasting reproach of the last verse the voices divide over its extent. Gill takes it as a just retaliation for bantering the word, and holds that it cannot be restrained to the seventy years of the captivity; Clarke likewise carries it down to his own day. Calvin sets a limit the others do not: such threatenings, he says, are restricted as to time and extend only to the coming of Christ, since the Church could not be doomed to a reproach without end, and God delivered his own when the Redeemer appeared, the words standing against the despisers rather than the people as such.
